title: Retreats
hook: a few days away for silence and prayer
tomorrow: Block close: the house of prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Camino, the long road to Santiago. Your line was buen camino. Who did you wish a good way? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

A weekend bag by the door, packed light. No laptop in it. Jesus once said to his tired friends, in Mark's Gospel: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." The next line explains why: "for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat." No time to eat. People coming and going, nonstop. Some Christians take that invitation quite literally. A weekend in the guest house of a monastery. A few days at a retreat center by a lake. One day in a borrowed room with the phone switched off and left in a drawer, and nothing on the schedule. Today: retreats.
screen: `NO LEISURE SO MUCH AS TO EAT.`
`A GUEST HOUSE, A LAKE, A DRAWER.`

segments.voice: First, Jesus did it himself. Mark says, in the King James Bible: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Luke adds: "And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." And before he chooses the twelve, Luke says, he goes up a mountain and "continued all night in prayer to God." Second, the surprise. Back in Mark, right after rest a while, they slip off by boat to a quiet place. But the crowd sees them go, runs ahead on foot, and is waiting on the shore. Jesus steps out of the boat, and Mark says he "was moved with compassion toward them," and began to teach. The rest was real, and so was the interruption. He held both. Third, how Christians go apart now. Some monasteries keep guest rooms, and visitors join the monks at prayer, eat in silence, and walk. Some retreats follow the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuits, with a guide who meets you each day. Some churches run weekend retreats with talks, singing and long walks. Some people keep a single quiet day at home. The forms differ. The shape is the same: leave the noise on purpose, for a while, and then come back. Last, why the silence. The prophet Elijah, worn out and hiding in a cave, waits for God on a mountain. A great wind tears at the rocks, "but the LORD was not in the wind." Then an earthquake, then a fire, and God isn't in those either. "And after the fire a still small voice." A voice that small is easy to miss in a wind. That's one reason people go on retreat at all.

Here's the practice: plan a quiet day. Settle, and breathe. Use these two minutes to plan one: a whole day, half a day, or a single quiet hour. Look at the weeks ahead and pick a date. Then pick the place: a church, a park, a library corner, your own kitchen with the phone put away. Decide what you'll leave behind. Decide what you'll bring: a Bible, a notebook, a walking route, nothing at all. If you pray, you can offer that day to God now, in your own words. If you don't, simply hold the date in mind and let it wait for you. The bell holds the time.
Retreats. Going apart on purpose, for a day or a few days, for silence and prayer, and then coming back.
Your line: come away awhile. Today, put your quiet day on the calendar, and guard one silent quarter hour before it comes. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Christians go on retreat at monastery guest houses, retreat centers and church weekends; some follow the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius with a guide, and others keep a single quiet day of silence, prayer and walking.

pairs: after the wind, earthquake and fire

myth: the Gospels never show Jesus taking time away
Mark and Luke both show him slipping off to solitary places to pray.
Elijah heard God in the great wind
"the LORD was not in the wind." after the fire came a still small voice.
in Luke, Jesus prayed all night before choosing the twelve
he "continued all night in prayer to God."

fork.setup: you're Jesus. you and your friends have finally slipped away by boat to rest. you step onto the shore, and a crowd has run ahead and is waiting. what do you do?
options: get back in the boat and find somewhere emptier.
send them home: you came here to rest.
have compassion on them, and begin to teach.
fork.reveal: Mark says he "was moved with compassion toward them" and began to teach. the rest was real, and so was the interruption.

original.note: Greek: a lonely, empty place, the "desert place" Jesus calls his friends to in Mark 6:31.

trapdoor: what you thought: a retreat is a getaway with fluffy robes.
what it means: going apart on purpose for silence and prayer, then coming back to the crowd.
what a scholar hears: eremos, the lonely place of Mark 6:31, where Jesus took his friends to rest, and where the crowd found them anyway.

notes: 'The twelve' is from Luke 6:13 ('of them he chose twelve'), cited.

Retreat forms (monastery guest houses, Ignatian Spiritual Exercises with a daily guide, church weekend retreats, a quiet day at home) are described with 'some'; confirm they are fairly described. Ignatius named as founder of the Jesuits; confirm.
Elijah 'worn out and hiding in a cave' summarizes 1 Kings 19:4–9; confirm.
The voice says 'And after the fire' with a capital A; the source quotes the KJV's lowercase mid-verse 'and after the fire'.
Original ἔρημος: confirm it is the word behind 'desert place' in Mark 6:31.

Editor pass: the hook now opens on a scene instead of a scripture quotation (three hooks in this range opened on a quote); 'Luke tells it as a habit' became 'Luke adds', since the KJV wording does not state a habit.

Audit (fresh reviewer): hook said 'people at the door from morning to night', which Mark 6:31 does not say; now follows the verse ('coming and going'). 1 Kings 19 'still small voice' also appears on days 1339 and 1354 in this block; Keeper may want a different closing image.
